transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-28
Start time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Anika Rao (BrightLane Eng Mgr), Tom Hayes (Backend), Priya Mehta (Product), Evan Cole (Security)

Summary:
Weekly poc sync focused on SDK integration patterns for function/tool calling and structured output. Reviewed current pilot results (latency/cost tradeoffs), discussed schema enforcement for deterministic outputs, and planned next round of benchmarks. Action items captured at end.

Topics:
- SDK hooks and invocation patterns (sync vs streaming)
- Function calling reliability and error handling
- Structured output schemas and validation at app layer
- Perf numbers observed in staging (latency percentiles, tokens)
- Security questions around tool permissions, KMS and logs

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Lena: All right, hey everyone thanks for joining, um we have about 45 minutes, we'll run through the last week's results and then Marcus will demo the variant bench runs we ran against the customer plugins.
[00:27] Anika: Thanks. Quick note, Tom couldn't make the first 5 but he'll be here in a couple minutes, he just pinged. We're mostly hoping to get clarity on the output schema enforcement and function fallback behaviour.
[01:05] Marcus: Cool, I can start with the bench quick. So we ran three flows: 1) plain text generation with streaming, 2) streaming + function calls where the model returns the call token stream then the app invokes the tool, and 3) batched sync with prefix caching. The interesting bit was the tail latency on the streaming function call case — it spiked when KV cache wasn't warm.
[01:39] Priya: When you say KV cache is not warm can you just, like, spell that out for us? We've got a mixed workload, some long conversations, some short queries.
[02:05] Marcus: Yeah so our runtime uses a KV cache for attention keys — sometimes transcribed as K V cash in the logs — when the cache miss happens the runtime has to refill the cache which adds a ~60-120ms penalty per refill depending on seq len. On the pilot traffic pattern this showed up a few percent of requests.
[02:44] Tom: Sorry I'm in — can you repeat the exact penalty numbers and the distribution? We saw a lot more variability on our side when sequence length jumps above 1k tokens.
[03:10] Marcus: Sure, p50 was steady at 180ms for streaming + function call, p95 moved from 420ms to 680ms on long sequences when the cache had to refill and when batching thresholds waited longer. The batching config we used for the bench was fairly conservative to prioritize latency.
[03:43] Anika: Ok that helps. Our acceptance bar is 500ms p95 for user interactive flows but we can tolerate 1s for background tasks.
[04:02] Lena: Good to know, and that informs whether you go hosted vs dedicated. For this POC it seems like dedicated with pinned instances would reduce those cache refill events, but we heard earlier you don't want to commit infra yet?
[04:24] Anika: Correct, we're still evaluating. The main blocker is security — Evan's team needs to validate VPC deployment and KMS integration.
[04:38] Evan: Right. Two quick asks: we need to know where audit logs are stored, and whether function/tool calls generate a separate entry with the payload redaction options. Also can the SDK restrict which external tools a running model can call (allowlist)?
[05:03] Marcus: Short answers — audit logs go to the control plane event stream and can be forwarded to your syslog/s3/kafka; we redact sensitive fields by default but you can configure token-level redaction. For tool allowlist the SDK exposes a call policy you can bind to the API key or route that restricts callable tool ids.
[05:38] Priya: Are those policies enforced at the runtime or in the control plane? We need enforcement even in Private/VPC setup.
[05:52] Marcus: They are enforced in the runtime assembly — the host checks the policy at invocation time. In private deployments we ship the policy engine as part of the private control plane so enforcement remains local.
[06:13] Anika: Great. Can we get the specific docs/practicals? We had trouble mapping the examples to our plugin code in the SDK.
[06:25] Lena: I'll send the SDK hooks doc and a short how-to repo link after the call. Deck: https://redwood.app/poc-hooks-deck and SDK repo snippet: https://redwood.app/sdk-examples (these are placeholder links used in the call notes).
[06:55] Marcus: Demo time — I'll share my screen — I'm going to replay the streaming with function call trace. Note: transcription may garble some log lines, sometimes 'K V cache' becomes 'K V cash' in the automated logs.
[07:20] [screen share noise] Marcus: So here's the call: model emits a function call structured object, our SDK turns that into a tool invocation. We tested two patterns: 1) auto-invoke where the SDK automatically calls the tool and patches the response into the continuation, and 2) manual callback where the app receives a function token and then explicitly calls the tool.
[07:56] Tom: Which pattern gave better latency?
[08:05] Marcus: Auto-invoke reduces one RTT but trades off observability — you end up with the tool call in the runtime logs but your app has less synchronous control. Manual callback is slightly slower but better for complex transactions where your app needs to validate or enrich the input.
[08:36] Priya: For us, we need deterministic structured output for billing and therapy notes — so manual callback sounds safer because we can run additional validation.
[08:52] Marcus: Agreed. Also for structured output we recommend embedding a small schema validation step client-side. Redwood's SDK offers a lightweight JSON schema validator hook that runs post-generation. It's not full type enforcement but helps catch obvious mismatches.
[09:18] Anika: We tried a similar validator but saw occasional shape drift where the model outputs a string instead of array. Any tuning tips?
[09:35] Marcus: A few: 1) add explicit examples in the prompt, 2) enforce output_format in the SDK call (structured:true, schema: { ... }), and 3) set a sampling temperature to 0.0 for critical fields. Oh and we have a quantization profile recommendation called 'float8-safe' that preserves numeric fidelity for structured outputs — the docs call it fwa, sometimes mis-typed 'f wa' in older notes.
[10:12] Evan: Does quantization impact token-level determinism? We have to ensure IDs and amounts don't scramble.
[10:25] Marcus: It can, if you choose aggressive quantization. The float8-safe profile avoids dropping precision in the final layers used for classification/structured tokens. For guaranteed determinism we recommended pinning a model variant with the same compilation kernels across the run — which is easier on dedicated or private.
[10:58] Priya: On the SDK integration surface, we ran into a problem where function call payloads exceeded our internal transport limit occasionally. Any suggestion?
[11:15] Marcus: Best practice: split large payloads into a blob reference (signed URL) and pass pointer in the function call. The SDK has a utility to upload payloads to your blobstore and inject a signed pointer. We have an example snippet in the repo.
[11:38] Tom: About error handling — if the tool invocation fails mid-flow does the SDK automatically do retries or bubble the exception? Our flows are idempotent but we need to know what behavior to expect.
[11:58] Marcus: The SDK has configurable retry policies with exponential backoff; by default function calls are retried twice for transient errors. You can also attach a compensating handler to mark the generation as 'tool_failed' and emit a structured fallback token so downstream services can handle it.
[12:28] Anika: That fallback token idea sounds useful. Do you have an example of the token shape?
[12:35] Marcus: Yep simple: {"status": "tool_failed", "tool_id": "search-v1", "error_code": "timeout", "fallback": "replan"} — again we will send exact sample shapes in the repo.
[12:58] Priya: On the app side we need to map these tokens to UI states, so consistent keys matter. Can we lock schema names?
[13:10] Marcus: You can lock them by pinning the schema in the route config; the runtime will reject mismatched keys if 'strict_schema' is enabled — but note that will surface generation rejections back to your app. Many teams prefer soft validation with alerts first.
[13:45] Lena: Quick commercial / logistics: earlier we discussed pilot duration and unit costs with the finance team — I will resend the latest pricing sheet. It includes hosted and reserved capacity estimates plus a short note on how batching and KV cache affect unit cost.
[14:03] Anika: Please include a sample cost projection for 1M tokens/month with 60/40 user/async split. That helps our procurement.
[14:17] Lena: Will do.
[14:25] Marcus: Back to tech — I want to call out a weird edge case we saw: when you combine streaming + auto-invoke with long-form tool outputs, the streaming buffer can deliver partial function args which the tool truncates, leading to malformed JSON in the tool input. The remedy was to buffer until end-of-call token or to use the manual callback pattern.
[14:56] Tom: Hmm we ran into that. Any immediate mitigation besides switching patterns?
[15:06] Marcus: Add a small framing wrapper in the SDK that assembles chunks into a complete JSON, check for balanced braces, then trigger the tool. Works well for most cases. We'll share the wrapper snippet.
[15:27] Anika: On security again, does the SDK or runtime support per-route RBAC? We have multiple teams and need separation.
[15:40] Marcus: Yes per-route RBAC is supported via our route config. You can bind policies to API keys and integrate SSO (SAML/OIDC). In private deployments those policies can map to your existing IAM.
[15:57] Evan: For auditability we also need tamper-evident logs — can the event stream be signed or hashed on write?
[16:09] Marcus: Currently logs are append-only with sequence integrity and we offer an option to deliver to an external immutable store (e.g., your S3 with Object Lock). The signing feature is on our roadmap but we can discuss customer-specific work for enterprise pilots.
[16:34] Priya: Anything on monitoring? We want token-level cost breakdown and per-route latency histograms in the console.
[16:46] Lena: Redwood Console provides token-level breakdowns per route/model including p50/p95 latency and batching efficiency. You can hook traces to your internal observability with traced request ids.
[17:02] Tom: Will the console surface mis-generation rates vs our test prompts? We want eval alerts if structured output regresses.
[17:15] Marcus: There's a quality-monitoring module in Redwood Optimize that tracks evals and alerts on regressions for configured prompts — tie it to your golden prompt set. We'll demo that in the next session if you want.
[17:36] Anika: Yes please, add that to next week's agenda.
[17:42] Lena: Noted — Redwood Optimize demo next week.
[17:50] Marcus: I'm going to run through the bench artifact now — slide 4 has the p95 comparisons. (background typing) So the manual callback pattern p95 was 520ms for typical sequences vs auto-invoke at 470ms but the variance with auto-invoke was higher.
[18:18] Tom: Can you attach the raw bench CSV? We want to run the same harness in our environment.
[18:24] Marcus: Absolutely — I'll upload bench.csv and the harness script. Bench CSV link: https://redwood.app/bench/ff-54721.csv
[18:40] Priya: Small question — for the JSON schema validator you mentioned, is it pluggable so we can use our internal schema library?
[18:52] Marcus: It's pluggable; the SDK validator is an adapter layer — you can supply a custom validator function. We'll include a sample adapter for Ajv in Node and one for jsonschema in Python.
[19:10] Evan: About deployment modes — if we go private, will the control plane still be reachable or is it an entirely air-gapped package?
[19:23] Marcus: We offer both: private control plane that can be run in your VPC with outbound-only telemetry options, and an on-prem fully air-gapped option where we'd ship bits for an internal install. For the POC most customers pick VPC with limited egress.
[19:45] Anika: For compliance, we need the SOC2 report and encryption-at-rest details.
[19:52] Lena: I'll share our SOC2 and encryption specifics. Action: Lena to share security pack.
[20:00] Marcus: Quick note on function payload size — you mentioned transport limits. The SDK's upload helper uses multipart for big objects and signed URLs for blobs; we can configure TTLs.
[20:14] Tom: We also need to know the cost delta for streaming vs sync per token — do you have a quick rule of thumb?
[20:24] Marcus: Rough rule: streaming with small chunks can bump compute overhead slightly due to more context switches, but it saves on perceived latency. Cost delta is typically 5-15% depending on your batching efficiency. We'll send a sample cost model.
[20:45] Priya: Are there any gotchas with function calling and tool chaining where one tool calls another?
[20:55] Marcus: Tool chaining is supported but you must manage idempotency and be careful with retries so you don't double-run side effects. Our SDK includes helper tokens to mark in-flight operations.
[21:10] Anika: Ok, let's talk timeline. We plan to decide on pilot expansion by mid-April. Can Redwood push the next benchmark and the security pack before then?
[21:22] Lena: Yes — Marcus will run the bench and I'll send the docs. We'll target early next week for artifacts.
[21:34] Marcus: One more demo note: when validating structured outputs we sometimes instruct the model to emit a 'validation_token' so the generator prints out a small checksum — that makes it easier to verify end-to-end. It's a soft hack but effective.
[21:55] Tom: Neat. We'll try that.
[22:05] Anika: Quick Q, how does Redwood handle version pinning for models used in a route? We need reproducible runs for audits.
[22:18] Marcus: You can pin both model version and compilation kernel set in the route config. We also support immutable snapshots so you can replay requests against the same environment.
[22:36] Evan: About logs and data retention — can retention be set per customer and per-route? We need 7 years for certain artifacts.
[22:49] Marcus: Retention is configurable per account and can be exported to your long-term store. Seven years is long but doable via S3/Object Lock or similar. We'll include a retention config sample.
[23:08] Priya: Any performance tuning we should try next?
[23:15] Marcus: Yes: 1) reduce batching wait time for interactive routes, 2) increase cache warmup via synthetic preloads for long sequences, and 3) try a quant profile that balances cost with structured fidelity. We'll include exact knobs in the bench notes.
[23:40] Anika: For the bench run you did, can you tag which runs used the 'float8-safe' vs 'aggressive-quant' profile?
[23:50] Marcus: I'll annotate the CSV with those tags.
[24:02] Lena: Let's go through outstanding questions we promised to answer: security pack, bench CSV, SDK repo hooks, pricing sheet, and a short demo of Redwood Optimize. Anything missing?
[24:16] Priya: Please add schema validator adapter examples in both Node and Python.
[24:24] Lena: Noted.
[24:30] Marcus: I'll upload the code snippets, and I'll also paste the small framing wrapper for streaming function args.
[24:44] Anika: One operational question: who will be our primary contact on Redwood for the pilot?
[24:51] Lena: I'll be AE lead for contracts and Marcus will be the technical SE contact. You can reach Marcus at marcus.chen@redwood.com.
[25:05] Tom: Cool. For the next call can we do a short runbook walkthrough — like 20 minutes — and then the Optimize demo?
[25:16] Lena: Yes, next week we'll do runbook + Optimize.
[25:22] Marcus: Any other tech items?
[25:28] Priya: One more — we need examples of fallback UX states tied to the 'tool_failed' token.
[25:35] Marcus: We'll include UI mapping examples.
[25:40] Anika: Ok, sounds good.
[25:45] [brief pause, note of people writing] 
[26:10] Marcus: Uploading artifacts now... (links posted) bench: https://redwood.app/bench/ff-54721.csv repo: https://redwood.app/sdk-examples/hooks.zip security pack: https://redwood.app/security/brightlane-pkg.zip
[26:35] Tom: Received, thanks.
[26:42] Priya: Quick nit — in your example the schema used 'entries' vs 'items', we prefer 'items' to match our UI, will that be easy to switch?
[26:52] Marcus: Totally - schema names are configurable per route, but if you enable strict_schema you'll need to be consistent across your training/eval sets.
[27:10] Evan: Also if we do a private deployment who's responsible for patching and security updates?
[27:21] Lena: For private we offer two modes: you manage infra and handle patching using our release notes, or we can operate the control plane under a managed contract. We'll include options in the enterprise addendum.
[27:41] Anika: Good. Any blockers on our side to run the bench? We need the harness to be runnable in our staging.
[27:50] Marcus: The harness is a small docker image; we'll provide a docker-compose and a quick-start script. Should be <30 minutes to run.
[28:05] Tom: We'll take it for a spin.
[28:12] Priya: On the structured output validation, do you recommend temperature 0 for all calls? That reduces creativity but increases stability.
[28:25] Marcus: For critical fields set temperature to 0, for contextual or summarization fields you can leave it higher. It's common to mix: temperature 0 for the function-calling fields, 0.7 for user-facing summaries.
[28:45] Anika: OK that's helpful.
[28:52] Lena: We're about halfway, let's move to scheduling next steps and recap the action items.
[29:00] Marcus: Action item recap: Marcus will run variant benches and upload CSV, Lena will send pricing + security pack, BrightLane will provide sample prompts and success criteria.
[29:18] Anika: Confirmed.
[29:24] Priya: Also add schema adapter examples and UI fallback states.
[29:30] Lena: Noted.
[29:35] [timestamp jump, end-of-call logistics] 
[29:50] Marcus: Quick question — any competitor tech you're evaluating in parallel?
[29:58] Anika: We're doing a light eval of Anthropic for safety and OpenAI for model diversity, but primary focus is on infra economics.
[30:15] Tom: We'll run the bench in our cluster and share results with Marcus.
[30:22] Evan: Please include threat model examples for function calling — we have concerns about tool lateral movement and data exfil.
[30:33] Marcus: We'll attach a short threat-model note.
[30:40] Priya: Can you also include an example that shows how to redact PII before logging?
[30:49] Marcus: Yes, we'll include a small middleware snippet.
[30:55] Anika: Great. If there are no other items let's capture next meeting time — same day next week?
[31:04] Lena: How about 2026-04-04 15:00 PT, runbook + Redwood Optimize demo.
[31:15] Anika: Works.
